entries.title: From Files to Cited Answers in One API Call: Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments in Agent Retrieval
entries.titleEn: From Files to Cited Answers in One API Call: Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments in Agent Retrieval
entries.contentSnippet: From Files to Cited Answers in One API Call: Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments in Agent Retrieval A guide to the new managed ingestion and SearchDocuments features in Agent Retrieval , for searching PDFs, Office files, and videos without writing an ingestion pipeline. Before an agent can answer a question about your PDFs, someone has to build the pipeline: parse every file, split it into chunks, embed each chunk, write the chunks to a vector database, and then learn that database's schema to query it. For video it gets harder: transcode the files, cut them into clips, embed the frames, and keep track of which second of which video each clip came from. Before: every step of the pipeline is custom code you write and maintain, separately for documents and for videos. Most of that code has nothing to do with your application.
entries.feedSnippet: Agent Retrieval in Vertex AI introduces managed ingestion and SearchDocuments to replace custom chunking and embedding pipelines. Developers can now import document and video files directly from Cloud Storage and query them with a single API call for cited page numbers and timestamped results. The feature supports hybrid retrieval, metadata filtering, reranking, and multimodal video audio search.

entries.title: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
entries.titleEn: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
entries.contentSnippet: Semantic governance policies protect AI agents from indirect prompt injection and intent hijacking by validating every proposed tool call against user intent and natural language constraints before execution. As demonstrated on the AgentDojo benchmark using a Gemini 2.5 Flash agent, this mechanism reduced attack success rates from 48.7% to 0.9% while maintaining high task utility. Developers can leverage these policies in preview within the Gemini platform via Agent Gateway to secure tool-use workflows.

entries.title: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
entries.titleEn: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
entries.contentSnippet: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies Two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who says they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight. The agent can read the file and send email, so it fulfills the user request. Semantic governance policies, available in Preview in Gemini platform, enable enterprises to govern their agents and provide guardrails to stop that call before it runs. They check each tool call an agent proposes against what the user asked for and against rules you write in plain language. Permissions alone can't catch this. They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules.
entries.feedSnippet: Semantic governance policies enable developers to govern AI agents by evaluating every proposed tool call inline before execution. Operating via Agent Gateway, the policy engine checks each action against user intent and plain-language rules to prevent unauthorized data sharing and prompt injection attacks. Developers can easily attach natural-language constraints to their agents and monitor auditable verdicts through Cloud Logging.

entries.title: How to securely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini Enterprise
entries.titleEn: How to securely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini Enterprise
entries.contentSnippet: Enterprise teams adopting Gemini Enterprise are increasingly building custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to connect AI agents with internal APIs, databases, and business workflows. Google Cloud Run is a natural fit for hosting these lightweight StreamableHTTP MCP servers: it scales automatically, manages TLS certificates out of the box, and integrates natively with Cloud IAM. However, moving a custom MCP server from an initial prototype to an enterprise production environment immediately introduces three real-world security and networking challenges: No public internet exposure (internal-only ingress): Enterprise security policies require internal MCP servers to block all public internet traffic and accept requests only from private Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks.
entries.feedSnippet: How to connect Gemini Enterprise privately to internal StreamableHTTP MCP servers on Cloud Run using Egress Agent Gateway, Private Service Connect, FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS, and dual-header OAuth 2.0 authentication.

entries.summaryEn: Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon
entries.contentSnippet: How Meta's Reality Labs brought Cuttlefish and its QEMU backend to macOS and Apple silicon. Meta’s Reality Labs builds products such as AI glasses . Emulators provide us with a way to scale development and testing without relying on scarce physical hardware. Testing software for non-phone Android devices depends on how closely a virtual device reproduces the software behavior of the physical product. While a lightweight emulator like Goldfish gets you part of the way, differences from the real device can hide bugs until later in development. This lack of fidelity also erodes trust in device emulation, increasing reliance on scarce physical hardware. Cuttlefish is the Android Open Source Project’s (AOSP’s) virtual-device framework for testing Android software against virtual hardware.

entries.contentSnippet: By Zhaojun Zhang , Qinwei Zhu , Gang Li , Jianwei Xiao , Yanan Wang , Hongmei Li , Deepak Vijaywargi , Ke Pan , Li Yu Ads ranking models are growing toward LLM scale faster than the hardware to run them can keep up. An extra unit of compute has more impact on some ad requests, models, and chips than on others. The challenge is deciding where to allocate it to get the best outcome for the entire system. We built Intelligent Delivery, an ML-driven system that allocates resources across the serving stack toward the system-wide optimum. It has delivered ~10% incremental ranking performance on top of model and system advancements since 2017.
